Otherwise it's gonna reboot And be stuck needing a password. If agents don't know this and don't see it coming back online, they'll think something's wrong." | "quote": "“three kinds of record:

•	a step, which a task saves about its own progress;
•	a task, which is work handed to a worker, with a reply you can wait for;
•	an event, which is a signal with no reply.

The rule that follows from that design:

•	A message inside one agent's own conversation is a step of that conversation. That covers your typed message, its reply and its tool calls.
•	A message that asks another agent to do work and expects a reply is a task on the receiver's queue, and the reply is its result. That holds for peers as well as for parent and child.
•	A message that only signals, such as "done", "approved" or "wake up", is an event.”

Yes, this is obviously the correct design we move forward with. When I mentioned parent and child, I was not citing design to you. I was paraphrasing what I could remember an agent telling me about the different kinds of records that Absurd keeps, and probably one of the agents was telling me a task is work handed to our worker with a reply it can wait for. And probably the agent used the terms parent and child to communicate to me about one agent giving work to another agent, expecting a reply. And how this type of record works in absurd And... what it would eliminate the need for... watcher scripts polling, et cetera.

Also, I don't think I said every other messaging option needs to be deleted. I said *retired*. All other messaging options—specifically, what is *advertised* to agents as messaging options and what is *available* to them. Some of it is upstream code, so I'm not saying we delete upstream code. We make the cheap path the only path, and make it the correct path.

When an agent goes to send a message, even if it tries one of the retired or unapproved avenues, the infrastructure routes it to absurd and/or comsnet. I don't want to say too much, 'cause I'm not looking at the code. I'm just speaking in hypotheticals, but this needs a proper Fable design pass.

Once everything's downloaded, all the upstream updates are reconciled and folded into the app, and we have an updated app, Fable needs to look at the code and architecture and actually see: What do we need to do to not incur tax with upstream message-related code, but also not allow agents’ messages a door outside of the absurd substrate and comsnet? I think likely we should approach this the way we are planning to approach the delivery seam. In the past, I tried to shape the way agents talk to me and format their messages and links using stop hooks, for example, and that turned out to be very expensive. The stop hooks would allow the message to be created, then refuse it if it's incorrect or not formatted properly, and force the agent to reproduce the entire message with updated formatting. This created at least double token spin, double token costs. The plan is for ThroughLine infrastructure to Have a delivery. Plain, seam. I don't remember the word we use, delivery something, delivery plane, delivery scene. The idea is that the infrastructure takes whatever the agent has produced, formats it for the agent, fixes things that are missing, and presents it to me in the chat the way I want it. If an agent's message is missing links or the links are wrong, this delivery—we'll say module for now—takes the message, fixes it, and delivers it to me correctly.

If there's genuinely something missing, like an agent said something vague where we require specificity, the infrastructure doesn't make things up. It can't make up a fact it doesn't have or doesn't exist. Instead of making the agent reproduce the entire message, the infrastructure would go back to the agent, tell the agent what's missing, and the agent can provide the delta. That would get appended to the message or posted after it as an appended message. That way, the agent's only producing the missing parts and details, not redoing things or having to remember formatting and links.

I think probably we'll have the same approach with messaging, where agents just try to send a message without having to think about doing it the right way or using the right tool. The system should just deal with it and get it into the right lane. It should just work for the agent, you know? All the agent knows is it sends a message, it gets to the agent ordered to me, and it receives messages.

And also, in your descriptions of the different records for agents, don't forget me. Don't leave me out of that. I want my messages treated like agents' messages. My role might be different, but I don't want a carve out to my messages that's different from agent messages. Maybe it's identified, sure. I've also spoke this to the lead agent: in the new messaging, whatever device I'm on—if I'm on the Mac desktop, if I'm on my Android phone, if I'm on iOS phone, if I'm on Linux Tower—wherever I'm sending messages from, I want my messages ID'd As me and also the device. So if I'm in this thread talking to you through my iPhone, through ThroughLine, this message should have a ID that says it's me on my iOS device, or me from the iOS device. I don't care about the semantics, just that it's identified that it's a message for me sent from my iOS device. Then, let's say the very next message I send you, I'm actually at my laptop. That message will still post to the same thread and say it's me, but it'll say it came from the desktop, not iOS. I want this distinction because if agents know I'm on my phone, they're not gonna be asking me to do things on the desktop, 'cause they'll know I'm not on the desktop, you know?

This is the only example I can think of, and where the idea started to percolate. I was talking to an agent through my iOS ThroughLine app, and I needed to rewind the agent. It produced a handoff document for itself and a kickoff prompt. Nobody told it to do this, but it was, I guess, trying to make things easy for maybe the both of us. Rather than give me the kickoff prompt in the chat in a code box, it posted a piece of code for me to run in the terminal on my Mac desktop. It would fetch the kickoff prompt and, I guess, expand it from the document and send it to my clipboard on the desktop so I could just paste it into the chat.

The agent thought it was being helpful by giving me just one line of code. All I had to do was run it, and the prompt would be in my clipboard ready to paste. But I'm reading this and thinking about how the agent doesn't actually know where I'm at. It assumed I was on the desktop, but I was on my phone. If I run that command on my phone, yeah, it'll add the prompt to the desktop clipboard, not my phone clipboard. I'm rewinding from my phone. I would need it in my phone clipboard.

These sorts of little details, I think, get worked out whenever it's more clear where I'm at. I don't think the agent would have given me that prompt if it knew I was on my phone, 'cause it would have thought about how to get me the prompt on my phone, and I don't think that's the solution it would have come up with. So that's an example of how, if it knew through the messages what device I was talking to it on, it would alter the choices it made.

Rules T3.01 enforces: (1) Prevention happens only before execution. A post-tool observation is recorded as observed-after-execution with prevented false; a building effect observed while check-first is pending is a recorded violation that stops the request and surfaces it, never counted as prevented.
